questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The biggest aspect of me choosing South Korea, was because I wanted to go somewhere where I really got a culture shock and would experience a completely different culture than mine, in a really special way through studying, which you can't really get anywhere else. Besides from this. had I heard and read others evalutions about Seoul and there were all really positive about it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was the best choice I have ever taken. This half year gave me so much, amazing friends from all over the world (mostly europe), an incredible insight in a new culture and country, which was so extremely exciting and beautiful. I can't stress enough how much I will recommend studying abroad, and especially in Seoul. The city is so exciting, so big that you will never will feel like you have seen anything, with so many cool, hip but also traditional korean areas.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I got my acceptance letter from SKKU really late, we all did, which was a bit stressful. But I knew how my schedule would look the first week, which was nice. Although I asked them a couple of questions and they never really responded to any of my e-mails. Though I found out everything once I had gotten there. But in general they are not as good informing their pupils as they are on KU.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I was invited to a exchange students event at my school, which was really nice, because it was the day after I arrived, so I quickly feel like I met other exchange students, and people were so eager to get friends you quickly feel like to know a lot of people. 
We also got told we would each get a buddy, a korean student, to answer any questions we might have, but we got this buddy so late that it didn't really matter.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was pretty easy for me, because I got recommend a shared housing community called Simple Spaces, by someone I know who had just been on exchange. She was really positive about the place, and me and two other Danes I had met through an asia exchange students event at KU, applied for this, and luckily we got it, because we applied in really good time. 
A lot of the other students at SKKU lived at the dorms, which is also really cheap and also seemed really social and nice for a lot of them. But you need to live with someone else, whom you don't know who is, and some of the dorms is actually really far away. But I had almost 1 hour of commute to school, so it depends on what you are prioritizing. I found it really nice to live in another area than my school, and that area (Haebangchon) ended up being my favorite in all of Seoul.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: As I said, it's really nice to live in another area, that you otherwise quickly only stay in the same area every day. Though it is more expensive than living at campus. But I found it so much nicer to have your own room, and to have more space to chill with your roomies and have people over for parties and stuff. You have a lot more freedom if you are living off campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think it would be nice if the school offered other living situations than dorms where you have a curfew, you can't bring anyone to your room, and you need to share your room with a stranger.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was really stressful to registrate for the courses. You needed to be totally prepared the minute the courses became available, and one course I really wanted, I didn't get.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You need to be ready at the minute. The system is pretty complicated where you need two different programs, to first put courses in your bag in one system, so that they are available for you to choose in the other system.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not really any kind, I talked to my future roomie in Seoul which luckily also studied at SKKU.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got four out of five. Although I actually changed my mind while signing up because I didn't get what I wanted and my friend got another one than me and stuff. Although in the end I ended up with the five courses I wanted, but it is also really hard in some courses to get a spot once everything is filled.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make a structured plan about which courses you would like to have before it starts. And also become comfortable with the programs and websites beforehand.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level is in general pretty low comparing to KU. When I think back on it now I feel like a had a gap year almost, the courses really didn't take up a lot of time and energy. Only one course out of five ended up being a little challenging, but were still easy compared to KU's level.
I loved it because I didn't come to learn and be better academic, but if this is your goal, you shouldn't pick the IEC courses (only for exchange students), and in general think more about which courses to choose.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was pretty different in the different classes. Two of my four professors weren't Koreans. But the culture were still similar to each other. The teacher were more 'the boss' or someone who is always right, than in Denmark. You would never call them by their first name. It was a lot of the professors talking in most of the classes, and we had at least one presentation, alone or in groups, in each course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
French cinema and cultural contents
Workshop for Experimental Film and Video
Contemporary Korean Society and Culture
Comparative Thought and Culture: Horizons East and West
Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights was pretty interesting with a decent teacher. It was the heaviest of my courses, as the exam was pretty big. But still, easy compared to DK, so you can easily manage it.

Contemporary Korean Society and Culture was also pretty interesting, with the nicest korean lady as our professor. She really cared about us having a good time, and not being too caught up in school and homework. This was really nice, and so easy!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Costs for Alien Registration Card, which is kind of like a license to be there. And just in general wa shopping groceries a lot more expansive than I thought, and the area I lived in was also pretty expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Fruits, some vegetables, rice, meat is also crazy expensive
Kimbap, noodles and small korean restaurant are really cheap and so nice.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I tried signing up for a dance class, but both of them at the school wasn't pen for exchange students:(

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of different classes. Sports, poetry, math, chess

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't know, I didn't try anything

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to other places in Korea! but also really explore everything you want to do in Seoul. I ended up only taking three trips somewhere else, because there were so many places, areas, sights I wanted to see in Seoul.
But go to different new areas you hear about, that may be 1-1,5 hour away, because it takes a long time to go everywhere in Seoul.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Pretty easy, not that I ever really got into it. But most people are used to 'tourists' and also because I was with other exchange students all the time, that helped me out to feel at home more quickly I think. 
But if you are somewhere where there are only older people, or really local, you cannot help but feel like a complete outcast and that you don't belong there.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Mhh, it's probably easiest in school. But even then, it can be a challenge. Most Koreans are terrified of speaking English, so they will probably just shake their head and look or walk away, if you try to encounter them. However one of my friends, who is really outgoing, got two different korean friends. But they started talking to her first as well, and then you know they are comfortable speaking English.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier - 100%. Also they party differently, not as much if they take their study seriously, and they have a lot more inhibitions. They won't really dance and stuff like that. But most people are really nice and helpful if they know how to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The temples, the food, the sharing-feeling and the feeling of community they have with each other. It's very different than in Denmark

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go into it with an open mind
You really don't need to know anything or be a k-pop fan to be going. I didn't have any of these interests and knew nothing, and don't worry - there are a lot of people like you, you are not only surrounded by k-pop lovers.
Don't plan to many visits from back home, sometimes it can be nice, but it also pull you out from the exchange bubble, which can be annoying, when you really want to be in that, and enjoy as long as it lasts. 
And!! don't be scared by the crazy different culture and language, it doesn't feel as alien, because you will be together with people who are in the same place as you, and who is really good at English.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If there are food you are going to miss which can be difficult or really expensive to get - bring it. 
Also deodorants, sun lotion (without whitening in it) can be difficult and/or expensive
Maybe learn hangeul - it will make your life a little easier.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To get to live in another country and really feel at home there. Have a complete network, regular places, a university and favorite areas and restaurants. That is really special.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I actually was really fortunate, I really didn't have a lot of challenges. I was so surprised of how not alone and homesick I felt. 
Though one thing, in one of my courses the language barriers were almost impossible to work with. That got me really frustrated, and I felt alone because I didn't know anyone in the course.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Please go!! It is an opportunity and experience that you will never get again.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
